Assessment Process The formal certification process involves an International Commission that verifies and progressively grants certification to countries. This process continues with ongoing surveillance until all countries are officially certified. Certification is only justified for diseases targeted for eradication, such as smallpox in the past and dracunculiasis, yaws, and poliomyelitis in the present. Validation of the elimination of a disease as a public health problem or verification of the elimination of transmission must be assessed against objective criteria within a country, area, or region, and the achievement must be formally recorded. Elimination, as defined by these criteria, is not a final endpoint but rather a status that must be maintained. The development and implementation of novel, effective interventions or surveillance and response systems may lead to future eradication. In such cases, countries that have validated or verified elimination as a public health problem or elimination of transmission would need to undergo the formal certification process under an International Commission. Validation of Kala-Azar Elimination in South-East Asia The WHO roadmap on neglected tropical diseases has set targets for eradication and elimination. Eleven diseases are targeted for elimination at the global, regional, or country level between 2015 and 2020. Process for Validating Elimination as a Public Health Problem, Verifying Elimination of Transmission, and Certifying Disease Eradication The WHO roadmap targets the eradication, elimination of transmission, or elimination as a public health problem at regional or global levels for diseases such as Chagas disease, human African trypanosomiasis, human dog-mediated rabies, leprosy, lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, schistosomiasis, trachoma, visceral leishmaniasis, and yaws by 2020. These targets are supported by global political commitments outlined in various World Health Assembly and regional resolutions. The definitions of elimination as a public health problem, elimination of transmission, and eradication of disease, as well as the indicators used to assess their achievement, are disease-specific and were established through a consultative process by WHO and its partners. WHO Roadmap Targets for Eradicating and Eliminating Neglected Tropical Diseases The roadmap outlines specific goals for eradication, global elimination, regional elimination, and country-level elimination for various diseases. For example, rabies elimination is targeted in Latin America and the South-East Asia and Western Pacific regions. Blinding trachoma elimination is targeted globally. Other diseases, such as yaws, leprosy, Chagas disease, and lymphatic filariasis, have specific elimination or eradication goals depending on the region or country. Standard Operating Procedures for Validation, Verification, and Certification Standardized procedures must be established for preparing, reviewing, and providing feedback on dossiers for validation, verification, or certification. These procedures include: 1. Preparation of dossiers by Member States, with WHO providing templates and technical assistance if requested. 2. Submission of dossiers to WHO for systematic review and assessment by a designated Reviewing Authority. 3. Feedback on dossiers, with WHO summarizing the Reviewing Authority's comments and decisions. 4. Official acknowledgment of validation, verification, or certification by WHO, including updates to the Global Health Observatory and publication in the Weekly Epidemiological Record. Post-Validation, Verification, or Certification Activities Member States must continue post-elimination surveillance for the disease based on its epidemiological characteristics. A statement of commitment and a description of the surveillance strategy should be included in the dossier. Stakeholders must recognize that the status of validation, verification, and certification is potentially reversible. If post-elimination surveillance data indicate a resurgence of the disease above defined thresholds, this change in endemicity status will be noted in the Global Health Observatory and the Weekly Epidemiological Record. Validation of Kala-Azar Elimination in South-East Asia In the WHO South-East Asia Region, kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is predominantly endemic in Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, with sporadic cases reported in Bhutan and Thailand. In 2005, a program was launched to eliminate kala-azar as a public health problem, setting a target of one case per 10,000 population at the sub-district level in Bangladesh and India and the district level in Nepal. Nepal has maintained this target since 2014, with other endemic countries in the region nearing the target. To assess progress toward achieving the elimination target, a formal process must be established to validate the elimination of kala-azar as a public health problem. This document outlines the steps and procedures to be followed for this validation process.
